title: Communication is key, inquest told
article: The inquest into the death of Jason Steacy, who was fatally shot by an OPP officer during an arrest in November 2005, wrapped up yesterday with the jury recommending measures to prevent future tragedies.
Topping the list was a recommendation that the OPP review protocols "to support effective communication" between police and paramedics in emergency situations.
On Monday, the inquest heard testimony from paramedics who were delayed in treating Steacy after receiving inaccurate information from ambulance dispatchers.
When paramedics arrived at the Elgin trailer park, they determined the address they were searching for did not exist.

It took 24 minutes to locate and then load Steacy into the ambulance, before rushing him to the Kingston General Hospital's trauma centre. Steacy lost vital signs while en route and was pronounced dead shortly after arriving at the hospital.
After deliberating for more than four hours on Tuesday, jurors spent the bulk of the morning yesterday finalizing their recommendations before delivering them to coroner Dr. Gordon Watt.

In the list of eight recommendations to the OPP and to the Ontario Ministry of Community Safety and Correctional Services, jurors addressed issues of front-line staffing in rural areas, the availability of equipment and resources, and also recommended a review of the OPP Records Management System.
"If any opportunities for greater efficiency or improvements are identified, the necessary adjustments should be made as soon as is practical," read the jury recommendation.
The jury also recommended that details of the case be incorporated into an Ontario Police College training module for new recruits.
In their recommendations to the provincial ministry, jurors called for a review of short- and long-term counselling services for police officers involved in cases where lethal force is used.
Vincent Clifford, the Ottawa lawyer representing OPP Acting Sgt. Brad Hollywood, who fired the fatal shot, commended the jurors yesterday.
"It was obvious from Sgt. Hollywood's emotional testimony that the psychological impact resulting from an incident involving the use of lethal force cannot be underplayed," said Clifford.
In his closing statement, Clifford told jurors that Steacy's death had "a profound effect" on the officers involved.
Watt, who presided over the eight-day inquest, assured jurors that the recommendations they made would be taken seriously.
"A true verdict is one that flows directly and logically from the evidence," said Watt, adding 70% of jury recommendations are implemented in some way.
The inquest was called in December after the province's Special Investigations Unit cleared Hollywood of wrongdoing.
